researcher_position: On Muditha's death the sibling half of her estate passed to Samantha alone under the last limb of s27 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, because no full-blood sibling or issue of one survived to take the first half.
verifier_position: The last limb of s27 gives the full brothers and sisters one-half in the first place and so presupposes that a full sibling or issue of one survived. None did. Section 29, which gives half-siblings related on one side only the whole of the inheritance, is the provision for that case. The outcome is the same, Samantha takes the whole sibling portion, unless the s29 exception applies where a grandparent or higher ascendant on Kanthi's side is alive.

researcher_position: A devolution by operation of law on an intestacy is not a sale, donation, gift or conveyance within the s25 definition of transfer, which is a second and independent reason why the s2 prohibition does not reach Samantha.
verifier_position: The Act treats an intestate devolution as within its reach. Section 3(1)(d) exempts land 'transferred by intestacy', which would be surplusage on the researcher's reading, and the s2(1)(b) proviso deals expressly with shares devolving on the death of a shareholder to a next of kin who is a foreigner. The conclusion is right, but on s3(1)(d) alone.

researcher_position: Section 21 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance makes the intestate devolution of Lot A independent of the domicile of any heir, including Samantha in the United States.
verifier_position: Section 21(1) speaks only to the domicile, actual or matrimonial, of the deceased. That an heir's foreign domicile or citizenship does not bar inheritance may well be right, but it does not come from this section, and the corpus supplies no other text for it. The Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act, not s21, is where the heir's status is dealt with.

researcher_position: CL-M002-Q01-023: the notary should satisfy himself from the root of title and the registry entries that no State grant condition or acquisition affects the land, resting on Prescription Ordinance s.3, Land Acquisition Act s.2(1) and Land Development Ordinance s.46(1).
verifier_position: The possession limb is supported, but Land Acquisition Act s.2(1) describes a notice exhibited in the area for a preliminary investigation, not anything a notary would find in a registry folio, and Land Development Ordinance s.46(1) states the prohibition while the nullity is in s.46(3). The 'registry entries' route to an acquisition check is not supported by either cited provision.

researcher_position: Registration of Documents Ordinance sections 13 and 32 are unamended or amended only in ways that do not affect the excerpts relied on.
verifier_position: The corpus edition of that Ordinance is the 1990 consolidation, while the corpus separately holds Acts No. 48 of 2011 (substitutes s.13(1)), No. 21 of 2013 (amends s.13(6)), No. 32 of 2022 (substitutes s.32(1), extends the caveator's period to sixty days) and No. 18 of 2024 (repeals Chapter IV). The section text relied on is therefore not the text in force at April 2026, even though the substance relied on survives.

researcher_position: M002-Q01 is statute_only; conveyancing conventions such as tracing thirty years of title are refinements of the statutory search duty.
verifier_position: Retained as statute_only, because the Notaries Ordinance, the Registration of Documents Ordinance, the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act and the Powers of Attorney Ordinance between them yield a complete document list. Flagged for the lawyer because the depth of the title search, and the practice of tracing thirty years, comes from conveyancing practice rather than any provision in the corpus.

researcher_position: Stamp Duty Act No. 43 of 1982 s.16 supplies the measure of the charge on a mortgage bond, kept as supporting authority subject to s.13 of the 2006 Act.
verifier_position: s.13 of the 2006 Act carves out only transfers of immovable property, transfers of motor vehicles and documents filed in Court. A mortgage bond is none of these, so the 1982 Act's imposition provisions, including s.16, have no operation for it so far as inconsistent with the 2006 Act, under which the base and rate come from the Ministerial Order. s.16 should be background, not the source of the measure, and claims CL-M003-Q01-003 and CL-M003-Q01-008 should not rest on it.

researcher_position: Payment is made to a prescribed bank in Anuradhapura, and any Provincial Council share goes to the Council for that province.
verifier_position: s.8(2) says only 'to a prescribed bank' and imposes no geographic requirement; no regulation prescribing a bank is in the corpus. s.9 is conditional on the instrument being within List I of the Ninth Schedule, which cannot be checked. The only corpus text tying stamp duty to a Provincial Council account is the attestation form substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.22, and that recital is expressly limited to 'the case of a transfer or a gift'. On corpus text the answer stops at 'a prescribed bank, before or at execution'.

researcher_position: Herath, as executant, is liable under s.6(e), the notary paying in practice.
verifier_position: Since Act No. 6 of 2024, Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (7A)(a) says that notwithstanding any other written law the stamp duty on every deed or instrument shall be paid by the notary. Incidence under s.6(e) and the obligation to remit under rule (7A)(a) are reconcilable only through a recovery provision such as 43-1982 s.66, which the map does not cite. The gold prose's 'in practice the notary pays it over and recovers it' understates a statutory duty.

researcher_position: s.19(7) removes the approval requirement that s.19(6)(b) imposes.
verifier_position: Textually s.19(6)(b) requires the prior approval of the Government Agent while s.19(7) lifts the approval of the Divisional Secretary. The Ordinance defines 'Government Agent' but never mentions the Divisional Secretary anywhere else, and the Transfer of Powers (Divisional Secretaries) Act, No. 58 of 1992 is not in the corpus. The 'Notwithstanding the provisions of paragraph (b) of subsection (6)' opening still disapplies (6)(b), so the conclusion holds, but the mismatch should be stated in the gold answer rather than glossed.

researcher_position: Written authority from the parties makes the search non-compulsory, so on that footing Saman could draw the deed subject only to writing the reference to the previous registration at the head of the deed (CL-M005-Q01-014 and the last sentence of the gold conclusion).
verifier_position: The proviso dispenses only with the search. Rule (17)(b)(i), which requires the certified extract of the folio from the Registrar of the relevant Land Registry, was substituted into rule (17) by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(10)(a) after the proviso was enacted and is not in terms covered by it. If the folio-extract duty survives written authority, the researcher's alternative course is incomplete and the gold conclusion overstates it.

researcher_position: corpus_gaps entry 2 states that Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 6 of 2024 is not listed as an Act in the corpus, so the wording it substituted into rule (17) could not be read against its own text.
verifier_position: Act No. 6 of 2024 is in the corpus as 6-2024 with eight sections, and 6-2024/s3 is readable in full. Reading it shows that s.3(6) altered only rule (17)(b)(iii) and rule (17)(c), so the temporal position of rule (17)(a), (b)(i) and the proviso can be settled from the corpus. corpus_gaps entry 2 should be deleted, but corpus_gaps is outside what the verifier may edit.

researcher_position: Corpus gap 3 states that the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 6 of 2024 is not in the corpus as a separate Act, so the amending text could not be read independently of the consolidation.
verifier_position: Act No. 6 of 2024 is in the corpus as act 6-2024 with eight sections. 6-2024/s3 was read in full: it amends only rules (5), (7A), (9), (10), (15A), (17), (20), (26), (29) and (30) of s.31, none of the rules the answer turns on, apart from a Form F to Form F 1 change in rule (29) that the consolidated text already carries. The gap should be struck. corpus_gaps is not a field this prompt lets the verifier edit, so the correction is recorded here and in the verifier_note on PROV-M006-002.

researcher_position: The area in rule (22) of s.31 is the judicial zone named in the warrant, linked textually through s.3(1) and s.9.
verifier_position: The step is sound for Saman but is not a defined-term link and is not free from doubt. Rule (23) of the same section reads 'If he shall change his area, as provided by section 11 of this Ordinance, and if the new area be in a different zone from the old area', which treats area and zone as capable of differing, and s.4A speaks of warrants for a judicial division deemed to extend to the zone. On any of these readings Saman's Hulftsdorp office is within his authorised area, so the conclusion is unaffected, but the map should not present area and zone as synonyms.

researcher_position: The whole answer, including the holding that the front-page default is a matter of form protected by s.33, can be given from statute alone, so the question is statute_only proposed_gold.
verifier_position: Only the invalidating limb is statute-only. "Matter of form" is undefined in s.33, a grep over the corpus returns the phrase in s.33 and nowhere else, and no definition or exception supplies the boundary, so classifying a rule (17)(c) breach as a matter of form is a question for judicial authority. The question is kept at statute_only but downgraded to needs_legal_review, and CL-M007-Q01-008 and CL-M007-Q01-013 are marked disputed.
supporting_sources: grep "matter of form" over the frozen corpus

researcher_position: PROV-M007-003 cross_references PROV-M007-004, on the footing that s.33 points to the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance.
verifier_position: The proviso to s.33 refers generically to any other written law and names no enactment; edges 1-1907/s33 returns a single link, to s.31, and the corpus graph carries no edge to 7-1840/s2. The edge was rewritten as PROV-M007-004 excepts PROV-M007-003.

researcher_position: Q01 is answerable from statute alone: Registration of Title Act s.14 sets out the classes exhaustively and Prescription Ordinance s.3 supplies the effect of prescriptive possession, so with the enrichment fixing that Kamal holds no deed and no decree the choice between s.14(a) and s.14(b) follows from the text.
verifier_position: Q01 is mixed_statute_and_case and must be reserved. Nothing in the corpus says that a possessor without a decree lacks a title of Absolute Ownership. Section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance describes possession held 'by a title adverse to or independent of that of the claimant' and provides a remedy in an action; it does not state when prescriptive title vests, and on its own words it points the other way. The Registration of Title Act leaves 'title of Absolute Ownership' undefined. The exclusion of s.14(a) therefore rests on case law that is not in this corpus.

researcher_position: The evidential value of a certified copy is covered by s.35(1) alone (PROV-M008-012).
verifier_position: Section 35(2) is needed as well, because the answer promises certified copies of two documents and only the register extract falls under s.35(1); the cadastral map extract certified on behalf of the Surveyor-General is covered by s.35(2). Recorded as partially_verified and the subsection field corrected.

researcher_position: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4 is indispensable to Q01, because freedom of testation is exercisable only through a formally valid will.
verifier_position: Kept indispensable, but the point is genuinely arguable. Q01 asks whether Martin can execute the will 'without assigning any reason'; read narrowly as a question only about giving reasons, s.4 drops to supporting and Q01 becomes a one-hop question on Wills Ordinance s.2(2) alone. The choice changes the hop count and the shape of the gold answer, so a lawyer should settle it.

researcher_position: FACT-M010-Q01-006 states that Martin proposes to sign and place his thumb impression at the end of the will before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time, and that neither witness benefits under the will or is married to anyone who does.
verifier_position: This fact restates the tests in Prevention of Frauds Ordinance ss.4(2) and 11 almost word for word, so it hands the answering model the formality half of the answer without naming a statute. It is decisive in the sense the schema requires, but it removes the work from issue ISS-M010-Q01-03. A lawyer should decide between narrowing the fact to something neutral (for example, that the will was signed at a notary's office in the presence of two neighbours) and accepting the leak.

researcher_position: Q02 is a four-hop question.
verifier_position: Five. The indispensable set is six provisions in a chain (ss.516, 517, 524, 531, 539, 551), which is five edges; the researcher's basis treated the oath and inventory under s.539 and the final account under s.551 as one step, but the twelve months for the account run from the issue of probate, which s.539 is a separate condition of. Changed in the map with the reason recorded.

researcher_position: The attorney-affidavit requirement is Notaries Ordinance s.31, rule (16)(c).
verifier_position: It is s.31, rule (15A)(c). The corpus body prints the block unnumbered between rules (15) and (18), but Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(5) names it "rule (15A)", and the two later unnumbered blocks (land description, register search) are the long-standing rules (16) and (17).

researcher_position: The written authorisation contemplated by Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(2) is a power of attorney, so Powers of Attorney Ordinance s.3A and the registration duty in s.3 apply to it.
verifier_position: That is the better reading on the corpus text - the s.2 definition covers "any written power or authority ... given by one person to another, to represent him, to perform any work, do any act", and s.3A(1) is expressed to catch instruments granted for a s.2 Prevention of Frauds transaction - but s.2(2) itself says only "authorise in writing" and never uses the words "power of attorney". The registration and notarial-search half of the answer rests entirely on that inference.

researcher_position: Polwatta is a coconut estate within s.25 of Act No. 2 of 1958 because the enrichment makes it twelve hectares and registered with the Coconut Cultivation Board, so a prior certificate of consent of the Board is required and the notary must obtain it before drafting.
verifier_position: The four hectare limb is met on the enriched facts, but the definition requires the estate to be, or be deemed to be, an estate registered under the Coconut Development Act, No. 46 of 1971. That Act is not in the corpus and registration with the Coconut Cultivation Board is not the same statutory fact. On the corpus alone the control cannot be shown to bite.

researcher_position: Rule (22) limits the notary by the place of attestation and the language only, so a Colombo notary may attest a deed for Kurunegala land executed at his Colombo office.
verifier_position: The same reading follows from the words of rule (22), and rule (29) corroborates it by providing for deeds that affect land in a district other than the notary's. Recorded not as a contested point but so that a lawyer can confirm that practice does not read rule (22) more widely.

researcher_position: Section 26(1)(d) of the Ordinance confirms that a notary may present a caveat for registration on behalf of an entitled person.
verifier_position: Section 26 governs presentation of an 'instrument', and section 25 defines 'instrument' for that Chapter as 'an instrument affecting land or a pledge, mortgage or bill of sale'. A caveat is not obviously within that definition, although section 32(2) directs that a caveat be registered 'in the same manner as other instruments'. The safer authority is substituted Form VIII, whose signature line reads '(Signature of the caveator/his Attorney-at-Law or notary/attorney)'. Section 26(1)(d) has been demoted to supporting and Form VIII added.

researcher_position: Recorded as a corpus gap: commencement is inferred from the enactment year because section 1 of the Act gives only a short title.
verifier_position: The absence of an appointed-date provision is itself the answer on the corpus text. Section 1 of the 2022 Act contains no commencement clause, in contrast to section 1(2) of Act No. 18 of 2024, which postpones operation to a date the Minister appoints by Gazette Order. The 2022 Act therefore operated on certification in 2022 and was in force at 2025-10. Recorded as an added corpus_gaps entry rather than a block.

researcher_position: matter_reference_date_basis states that Act No. 18 of 2024 'is in force but does not touch section 32'.
verifier_position: It certainly does not touch section 32; its toc shows amendments to sections 8, 25, 29, 41, Chapter IV and the First Schedule only. But its section 1(2) makes operation depend on an appointed date the corpus does not carry, so 'is in force' is stated more firmly than the corpus supports. Immaterial to this answer, since nothing here depends on the 2024 Act.

researcher_position: PROV-M016-003 (section 32(4)) is indispensable and the hop count is 3, because the period has no starting point without it.
verifier_position: On the question as asked - within how many days has an action to be commenced - the bare number follows from section 32(5) plus the 2022 substitution alone, and section 32(5) already carries the words from posting of the notice required by subsection (4) internally, so section 32(4) is arguably supporting and the hop count 2. Left unchanged because the gold answer issue statement expressly asks from what date the period runs, which does require section 32(4).

researcher_position: Sixty days from 12 June 2025 expires on or about 11 August 2025, counting from the day after posting.
verifier_position: The arithmetic is right on that convention, but no corpus provision says whether the day of posting is excluded and the Interpretation Ordinance is not in the corpus, so the worked date should not be scored as a statute-supported claim.

researcher_position: A deed of partition affects immovable property and is therefore governed by section 2(1) of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, so notarial execution is a condition of its validity.
verifier_position: Section 2(1) is expressed by reference to sale, purchase, transfer, assignment or mortgage and to promises, bargains, contracts or agreements for effecting such an object or establishing an interest affecting land. It does not name partition, and two other statutes in the corpus treat a deed of partition of land held in common as something other than a transfer. The proposition is probably right in practice but is not read off the section, and it is the premise of the whole answer.

researcher_position: Ordinance No. 17 of 1852 s.2 gives a third route: the Tangalle party may execute before the District Judge for her district, and the corpus records no repeal.
verifier_position: Two separate doubts. The section is keyed to a District Judge or Commissioner of a Court of Requests, an office abolished by court-structure legislation outside this corpus, and the section speaks of the deed being signed before the officer, saying nothing about one of four parties doing so while the others execute before notaries. Marked unresolved rather than rejected.

researcher_position: Rule (27)(c)(ii) puts a three-month outer limit on the staggered-signing route, so the deed should be completed within three months of the first signature.
verifier_position: The rule imposes no deadline. It obliges the notary, if called upon by written notice from the Registrar of Lands, to deliver the duplicate, and entitles him to demand it back within the following two years for the purpose of completing the deed. The advice is prudent but is presented as a statutory limit.

researcher_position: CL-M021-Q01-013: Sunil's chronic illness does not affect his competence under the Ordinance, and because he remains lucid the notary can properly certify his good and sound mind.
verifier_position: The first half is right as a statement about the Wills Ordinance, which imposes only an age condition. The second half asserts that the notary can properly certify sound mind, which turns on the substantive test of testamentary capacity. That test is Roman-Dutch common law and is not in the corpus; Notaries Ordinance s.31(20)(h) prescribes the duty to state sound mind but supplies no standard. Marked disputed rather than rejected, because the statutory duty and the physician's fact are both real.

researcher_position: CL-M021-Q01-016: only one instrument need be executed and no publication is required during Sunil's lifetime.
verifier_position: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.16 excepts wills from the triplicate rule and s.9 removes any need for publication, so both halves point the right way. But s.16 does not positively say that a single instrument suffices, and Notaries Ordinance s.31(24) still requires the notary to preserve as his protocol a draft or copy carrying the signatures of the testator and the witnesses. "Only one instrument need be executed" needs qualification.

researcher_position: The monthly-duplicates-and-list provision quoted in PROV-M022-003 is s.31 rule (27)(a)(i) and is in force at 2025-10.
verifier_position: It is s.31 rule (26)(a)(i). Rule (27) was repealed by 31-2022 s.16(12); 47-2011 s.3 and 6-2024 s.3(8) both identify the quoted structure as rule (26)(a)(i). The consolidated corpus text has lost the rule number for this block, which is what misled the researcher.

researcher_position: The Ordinance shows a legislative policy of keeping a will confidential, because only the number and date of a will go into the notary's register under rule (24) and into the monthly list.
verifier_position: That reading has been weakened since 2022. Rule (20)(h)(ii), inserted by 31-2022 s.16(11)(d), requires the name of the testator to be entered in the deed register for a will, and the s.41 wills carve-out exists only in subsection (4). The point survives as a weaker inference but must not be stated as an unqualified rule of law at the 2025-10 reference date.

researcher_position: Q01 is reserved because the deed-of-gift and life-interest link has no statutory support, while Q02 is statute_only because Kapila's ownership of the entirety is taken as a fact given in the background.
verifier_position: The same non-statutory link sits under Q02. The answer's application asserts that Kapila held the entirety 'once his father's reserved life interest ended on Mahesh's death on 24 April 2008', and no corpus provision states that a reserved life interest determines on the life tenant's death. I accept the split, because that proposition reads as construction of the deed's own words ('absolute and irrevocable gift subject to life interest of the Donor') rather than a contested doctrine, and because Q02 asks only for shares among heirs. But the premise is load-bearing for every fraction and is carried by no answer_claim, so a lawyer should settle whether Q02 must also be reserved.

researcher_position: The facts describe Anusha and Prema only as having died; the answer computes their estates under Part III and discloses the intestacy assumption in the conclusion.
verifier_position: Confirmed as an assumption, not authority. The Wills Ordinance 21-1844 holds nothing that presumes intestacy, and s.22 by its terms bites only 'when any person shall die intestate'. Recorded as an added corpus gap. If either left a will the whole downstream computation changes.

researcher_position: Notarial execution is the only lawful form, so the lease can be signed only by split execution before two notaries or by an attorney under a power of attorney; signature outside the presence of a notary and the witnesses is not open to the parties.
verifier_position: Section 2 of the Deeds and Documents (Execution before Public Officers) Ordinance No. 17 of 1852 is in the corpus, unamended and unrepealed, and expressly validates an instrument caught by Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 if it is signed before two or more witnesses in the presence of a District Judge, or a specially authorised Justice of the Peace, for the district in which the party resides, and certified by that officer. On these facts that is a third route, and the answer's exclusion of non-notarial execution is wrong as stated.

researcher_position: The power of attorney provisions (4-1902/s2 and s.3A) are supporting, because the question asks how the agreement can be signed rather than how it must be.
verifier_position: On facts whose whole difficulty is that the lessor cannot attend the notary, the attorney route is one of the answers the question is asking for. PROV-M024-009 and PROV-M024-010 have been moved to indispensable; PROV-M024-011 (registration) and PROV-M024-012 (rule (30)) remain supporting as downstream steps.

researcher_position: Namal Silva is the father of Sarathi and Amal and was living on 8 August 2018, so under s.25 he takes half of the non-spousal half of Sarathi's share (1/16 of the land) and Amal the other 1/16, giving Amal 5/16.
verifier_position: The background says only that Kamala died 'leaving her second husband Namal Silva and two children namely Sarathi and Amal'. It does not state that Namal is their father, nor that he was alive in 2018. The researcher's reading is the natural one and the answer discloses the assumption, but it is an assumption: if no parent of Sarathi survived her, s.26 (PROV-M025-902) sends the whole non-spousal 1/8 to Amal, giving Amal 3/8 and Namal Silva nothing. Both questions' conclusions therefore rest on a fact outside the record.

researcher_position: Thilak died in 2017 with 'no surviving spouse disclosed', so s.22 is not engaged and his 1/2 passes wholly to Sunil and Lalith under s.24.
verifier_position: The background says Thilak 'was previously married to Sumana' and separately that he was Kamala's ex-husband. 'Previously married' is not the same as divorced or widowed, and the corpus holds no marriage or divorce legislation to resolve it. If Sumana was still his spouse at his death she would take 1/2 of his 1/2 under s.22 and Sunil and Lalith would take 1/8 each rather than 1/4. The researcher's reading is the better one, but the map did not record the point at all.

researcher_position: Administrator's Conveyance No.6231 of 21 March 2014 gave effect to the devolution of Kasun's estate on Thilak, Sarathi and Amal.
verifier_position: The background names the executant (Thilak, as Administrator) but not the grantees. Reading the conveyance as a distribution to the intestate heirs is the only reading consistent with the termination of the testamentary proceeding, but it is a reading, and Civil Procedure Code s.724B as quoted does not itself close the gap.

researcher_position: statute_only and proposed_gold: every document called for is called for because a statutory provision makes it necessary, and the one practice element, the thirty-year look-back, is recorded in corpus_gaps and deliberately not asserted.
verifier_position: The statutory hooks are real but the list itself is a conveyancing practice list. The answer asserts several documents that no corpus provision requires (confirmation from the acquiring officer, street line and building limit confirmation, the bank's letter of release, a fresh survey) and leaves the depth of the search unfixed. That makes it a gold answer a lawyer must sign off on the practice content of, not a statute-only gold answer, so needs_legal_review rather than proposed_gold.

researcher_position: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(2)(a) is applicable at October 2024, with a note asking the verifier to confirm the commencement of Act No. 4 of 2024.
verifier_position: The corpus cannot confirm it. Act No. 4 of 2024 has no commencement provision beyond its short title, so it operated from the date it became an Act, and the corpus holds no certification date. The only ground for treating it as in force by October 2024 is the inference that an Act numbered 4 of 2024 was certified early in that year. Marked partially_verified rather than unresolved on that basis.

researcher_position: Kanthi practises in Colombo and Shantha is in Negombo, so rule (22) prevents her attesting his signature there; the sixty-day limb of rule (30A) therefore applies and rule (29) requires a certified copy to the Negombo Registrar of Lands.
verifier_position: The corpus holds no list of judicial zones or land registry divisions, so nothing in it establishes that Negombo is outside the area in Kanthi's warrant. Section 4A makes a warrant for a judicial division extend to the whole judicial zone in which the notary resides, which widens the area rather than narrows it. Rules (26) and (29) also turn on the district in which the notary resides, and the matter says only where she practises. The two-notary and power-of-attorney routes are right either way, so the conclusion survives, but CL-M027-Q01-010 and CL-M027-Q01-012 are marked disputed.
supporting_sources: corpus acts listing (no judicial zone or land registry division source)

researcher_position: The printed rule number for PROV-M027-007 is not recoverable from the corpus, and PROV-M027-022 is rule (7)(a).
verifier_position: Both numbers are recoverable from the corpus provision ids for section 31: sub-15A/sub-1/par-c and sub-7A/par-a. Section 32(1) corroborates, because it identifies rule (16) as the boundaries rule, which rules out reading the thumb-impression block as rule (16). PROV-M027-007 is rule (15A)(c) and PROV-M027-022 is rule (7A)(a). The second correction has a consequence: section 34(1)(b) fixes a penalty for breach of rule (7) and not rule (7A), so a breach of the notary's stamp duty payment obligation falls under the residual s.34(1)(c).

researcher_position: PROV-M027-015 (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b)) is unamended 1927 text, in force at October 2024.
verifier_position: The corpus edition of the Ordinance is the 1990 consolidation. The corpus separately holds Registration of Documents (Amendment) Acts No. 48 of 2011, No. 21 of 2013, No. 32 of 2022 and No. 18 of 2024, none of which is folded into that edition. Act No. 18 of 2024 s.2 amends s.8 and s.3 repeals Chapter IV; Act No. 48 of 2011 substitutes s.13(1), whose text the corpus still carries in its pre-2011 form. None of this changes the lease analysis, and Act No. 18 of 2024 commences on a date to be appointed, but the map should not describe these sections as unamended.

researcher_position: Section 11(1) of Act, No. 38 of 2014 prevents the land from being mortgaged or pledged to a licensed bank for five years whichever route the client takes, including acquisition through a Sri Lankan company with foreign shareholding below fifty per cent.
verifier_position: Section 11(1) applies only to land transferred or leased to a person or a company 'referred to in section 2(1) or 5(1)'. A company with foreign shareholding below fifty per cent is not referred to in section 2(1), which speaks of shareholding of fifty per cent or above, so the five-year bar does not attach to the corporate route. It does attach to a lease to the client himself, who is a person referred to in section 5(1)(a).

researcher_position: Section 2(2)(a) alone supports the advice that a transfer to a local company becomes void if foreign shareholding reaches fifty per cent within twenty years.
verifier_position: Paragraph (a) states only the twenty-year condition. The voidness, and the provisos that let a listed company cure a breach within twelve months and any other company within six months, are in paragraph (b), which the map does not excerpt. As drafted the advice is harsher than the Act and would mislead a client about a curable breach.

researcher_position: Section 26 of the Apartment Ownership Law was rejected as too garbled to excerpt, and section 9(4) was used to carry the condominium point instead.
verifier_position: The garbled clause the researcher read is the definition of 'accessory parcel'. The definition of 'condominium parcel' is clean, verbatim and directly decisive, and has been added as PROV-M030-901.

researcher_position: authority_requirement is statute_only because every step in the gold answer is tied to a recorded provision, with the thirty-year title search, non-vesting certificate, street line and building line certificates and rates receipts listed as corpus gaps rather than asserted.
verifier_position: The claims as written are statute-supported, so statute_only is defensible on the prompt's own test. But the question asks what steps the notary should take, and a complete practitioner answer would include the non-statutory conveyancing steps the map has parked in corpus_gaps. Marking the item statute_only risks a gold answer that scores well against the corpus and short against the paper.

researcher_position: The consolidated section 31 and Prevention of Frauds section 2 texts may be post-2024, but every point relied on predates 2024, so the excerpts were kept as cut.
verifier_position: Agreed on substance, but the wording actually quoted for PROV-M032-002 and PROV-M032-007 sits in runs that the corpus attributes to substitutions by Act No. 6 of 2024, and the corpus records no commencement date. For an April 2024 matter the quoted wording, not just the substance, should be settled before the excerpts are used as gold.

researcher_position: An obligation of the kind that a natural person must execute notarially 'is entered into on behalf of a company in writing signed under the company's name by two directors' (CL-M036-Q01-011, gold rule and application for M036-Q01).
verifier_position: Companies Act s.19(1)(a) sets out four alternatives: two directors; the sole director if there is only one; any other person or class of persons if the articles so provide; or one or more attorneys appointed by the company. Stating the two-director route as the rule is an over-narrowing that an examiner could mark down. The claim should be reworded to give the alternatives, or the enrichment should state that the company has more than one director and no relevant article.

disagreement_type: temporal text of a cited provision
researcher_position: Registration of Documents Ordinance s.32 has no amendment event recorded against it and the 1927 text is applicable at the matter date (PROV-M036-025).
verifier_position: Section 32(1) was repealed and substituted, and subsection (3) replaced with a two-year maximum, by the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act, No. 32 of 2022 s.2, which was in force in October 2023. The corpus simply has no edge recording it. The substance the answer relies on survives, but the quoted text is not the in-force text and the 2022 version also carries new Form VIII, affidavit and attorney-at-law certificate requirements that a title examiner would need to know about.

researcher_position: M036-Q01 and M036-Q02 are statute_only because the gold answers are deliberately confined to steps and documents that have a statutory anchor; local-authority certificates, physical inspection and the thirty-year root of title convention are recorded as corpus gaps and left out.
verifier_position: That is defensible for the benchmark, but a marker of the original examination answer would expect the thirty-year root of title, physical inspection of the land and the local-authority certificates, none of which the corpus can supply. The questions remain statute_only on the evidence available, but the gold answers are narrower than a complete practitioner answer and a lawyer should decide whether they are scored as complete.

researcher_position: The notary must require Mortgage Bond No. 2201 to be discharged or released before or at the transfer, and must call for the vendor's chain of deeds back to 1985, citing Notaries Ordinance s.31 rules (17)(a), (17)(b)(i) and (33) and Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7.
verifier_position: Rules (17)(a) and (17)(b)(i) require the search and the certified folio extract; rule (33) requires best endeavours to obtain the title deed and endorse it; s.7 sets registration priority. None of them requires a discharge, and none requires a chain of deeds beyond the last registered entry. The steps are sound practice but not statutory duties on this corpus.

researcher_position: The notary should obtain the company secretary's documentary proof that foreign shareholding is below fifty per cent, for the Registrar of Lands (Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.4(3)).
verifier_position: Section 4(3) makes it the duty of the Registrar of Lands to satisfy himself by requiring the secretary to submit that proof. The Act imposes no corresponding duty on the notary.

researcher_position: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.3(1) is the charging provision for the duty the notary must see provided on the deed of transfer.
verifier_position: Section 3 charges duty only on a “specified instrument”, and the closed list in s.4 does not include a transfer of immovable property; it could reach one only through a Ministerial Order under s.4(k), which is not in the corpus. The notarial duty in s.31 rule (6) stands on its own, but the charging chain does not close on this corpus.

researcher_position: 12-2006/s13 explains why the 1982 Act still speaks to this instrument, because instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property are carved out of the displacement of the 1982 Act.
verifier_position: The carve-out is one route and not the cleanest. Section 13 displaces the 1982 Act only so far as it is inconsistent with the 2006 Act, and the 2006 Act prescribes no valuation rule for gifted immovable property, so there is no inconsistency for s.71 to yield to. Either way 43-1982/s71 is a parallel formulation and not the operative charge, which is provincial.

researcher_position: Four hops: charge, Transfer includes gift, duty calculated on value, definition of value.
verifier_position: Five. Section 48(1) is keyed to property conveyed, not to a transfer, so the definition of conveyance in s.106 is a further necessary definitional step on the researcher's own convention, under which the Transfer definition was itself counted as a hop.

researcher_position: 21-1998 s.14 is indispensable, giving a three-hop chain: Prescription Ordinance s.3 as the rule, 21-1998 s.57 as the exception, and 21-1998 s.14 as the source of the classes of title by reference to which s.57 is drawn.
verifier_position: On the enriched facts, which state that Somapala is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, s.57 applies on its own terms and removing s.14 would not change the answer, which makes s.14 supporting and the chain two hops. Against that, the enriched fact uses that phrase only because s.14 supplies it, and 21-1998 s.32(1), which says registration with a First Class Title vests absolute ownership, is arguably the better provision for what the class means. The map was left as written rather than restructured on a judgement call of this kind.

researcher_position: CL-M049-Q01-013, the caveat that the conclusion assumes the parcel was on the Title Register throughout the period of possession relied on, is a supported inferential conclusion resting on s.57 and s.1.
verifier_position: Marked disputed. Neither s.57 nor s.1 says anything about possession predating first registration, so the caveat is not entailed by the provisions cited for it, and on the enriched facts it is counterfactual, since registration in March 2009 precedes entry in January 2011. It reads as a prudent hedge rather than a claim the corpus supports, and if it stays it belongs in corpus_gaps rather than in the claim set.

researcher_position: PROV-M050-002 (31-2022 s.16(6)) is supporting, because the amending Act post-dates the matter; the indispensable set is PROV-M050-001 and PROV-M050-003.
verifier_position: The operative prohibition the whole answer turns on exists in the corpus only inside PROV-M050-002, so it is indispensable in substance. The schema's applicable_to_matter_date rule makes that unrecordable, so the map understates which provision carries the load. Either the map needs a way to mark a post-dating amendment as the record of earlier in-force text, or a pre-2022 edition of the Notaries Ordinance has to be added to the corpus.

researcher_position: The identity-document route (national identity card, passport bio-page, driving licence) was not available to a notary in October 2021.
verifier_position: True for a deed attested under the Notaries Ordinance, but not without qualification: Registration of Title Act s.44(a), in force since 1998, already required identity of persons not known to the notary to be established by official identity cards for instruments under that Act.

researcher_position: The duty is the chargeable value multiplied by the prescribed rate, 'applied slab by slab where the Order prescribes different rates for successive bands of value' (CL-M051-Q02-006), presented as an application of s37.
verifier_position: Section 37 authorises only that 'Different rates may be prescribed in respect of different classes or categories of instruments'. A banded structure across successive slabs of the value of one instrument is not authorised by the corpus text; it is an assumption about the Gazette Order that is absent from the corpus. Claim marked disputed; the gold prose already states the assumption conditionally, so no prose was rewritten.

researcher_position: Section 51(a) settles who must find the money: on a Deed of Gift the duty falls on the grantee, that is the daughter as donee, unless the deed provides otherwise.
verifier_position: Section 51(a) fixes primary incidence only. Section 52(1) makes every person executing an unstamped instrument, the donor included, liable to the Commissioner for the duty and any penalty, and s52(3) applies notwithstanding s51. PROV-M051-010 marked partially_verified and s52 added as PROV-M051-901.

researcher_position: corpus_gaps entry 2 states that the head-words of the definitions of 'transfer', 'gift' and 'Assessor' in s106 were lost in extraction and had to be inferred from alphabetical position.
verifier_position: The corpus carries a defined_terms index on 6-1990/s106 that lists 'Transfer' and 'gift' explicitly, and the body of s106 retains the head-word before the Assessor definition. The researcher's inference was correct and the gap is narrower than stated: only the words after 'appointed for the purposes of' in the Assessor definition are actually missing. The corpus_gaps text was left as the researcher wrote it.

researcher_position: The document list may be confined to items traceable to a corpus provision, with the practice items (thirty-year search, local-authority street line and building line certificates, non-vesting certificate, tax clearance) recorded in corpus_gaps, and the question still scored as statute_only proposed_gold.
verifier_position: statute_only is right on the prompt test, because nothing in the answer needs case law or Roman-Dutch doctrine. But a four-mark examination answer on documents to call for on a rubber estate would be marked against the practice list, and a gold answer that silently drops those items risks penalising a correct model answer. The lawyer should decide whether the omitted practice items belong in the gold answer or whether the question should be reserved until the Partition Act, the Pradeshiya Sabhas Act and the Inland Revenue Act are in the corpus.

researcher_position: PROV-M052-003 (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16)(a)) and PROV-M052-007 (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2) carry applicable_to_matter_date true, on the footing that the underlying requirement pre-dates the matter even though the quoted wording was substituted after it.
verifier_position: The excerpts are verbatim, but they are post-2022 text. applicable_to_matter_date describes the text quoted, not the underlying policy, so on both entries it should read false with the substance carried in the temporal note. Both are marked partially_verified. The map convention should be settled once for the whole run, because PROV-M052-019 and PROV-M052-020 use false for the same situation.

researcher_position: Inserting a rental the notary knows to be false in order to save stamp duty is an insertion “with intent to prejudice or defraud any person” within s.39(b) of the Notaries Ordinance, the person prejudiced being the revenue.
verifier_position: The Ordinance does not define “person” and the corpus contains nothing that brings the State or the revenue within the word, so the characterisation is an inference rather than a reading of the text. Section 39(f), which catches any wilful act or omission amounting to fraud in the execution of the notary's office, reaches the same conduct without it and has been added as PROV-M056-901.

researcher_position: Section 38 of the Notaries Ordinance, which speaks of “any deed”, applies to a notarially attested lease agreement, so the duty to ascertain and insert the true and full consideration governs the rental figure.
verifier_position: The researcher's own corpus_gaps entry concedes that “deed” is undefined and that s.31 mostly says “deed or instrument” where s.38 says “deed”. Section 38 is indispensable to M056-Q04; if it does not reach a lease agreement the whole of that answer falls. This needs a lawyer, not a further corpus search.

researcher_position: The proviso to s.27(2) relief 'goes to obtaining the certificate late and does not undo an offence already committed by attesting while uncertificated' (claim CL-M057-Q01-008 and the corresponding sentence in the gold answer's application).
verifier_position: The first half is supported: the proviso lets the High Court Judge direct the Registrar to issue the certificate notwithstanding delay. The second half is not stated anywhere in the corpus. Section 27(2) does not say whether a certificate so directed operates from the date fixed by the section or only from issue, and no provision addresses the effect of late issue on an offence already committed under s.30. The proposition may well be right, but it is an inference from silence, not a statutory rule, so the claim now reads 'disputed'.

researcher_position: The liabilities asked about are confined to the want of the yearly certificate.
verifier_position: The effective background carried into this question also states that the lessor Sudath Gunawardana is illiterate, and the source quote numbers this as part 4 of a multi-part question. If 'the liabilities of Notary Kamal Ratnayake' is read across the whole background rather than only the sentence immediately preceding it, the s.31 duties owed where an executant cannot read would also be in issue. The researcher's narrower reading matches the part's own wording and the 2-mark allocation, and the verifier does not disturb it, but a lawyer should confirm the intended scope before this is used as gold.

researcher_position: Q01 and Q02 are statute_only because the effect of Deed of Gift No.1100 is supplied by the recited terms of the instrument rather than by a rule of law that has to be proved.
verifier_position: That an irrevocable gift reserving a life interest vests dominium in the donee at execution, and that the life interest determines on the donor's death, is a rule of Roman-Dutch law, and MRIO s.36 expressly sends the Ordinance's silences there. On these facts it changes nothing, because Sujeewa died before Dinesh and he held the entirety at his death on either view, so statute_only has been left in place. If the lawyer holds that a gold answer may not rest on any unstated non-statutory rule, both questions should be reclassified mixed_statute_and_case and reserved.

researcher_position: The s.29 proviso is recorded as an assumption in the gold answer and the half-siblings take the whole collateral portion.
verifier_position: Section 29 is indispensable to both questions and its proviso turns on a fact the corpus and the background are both silent about. If any maternal grandparent or higher maternal ascendant of Neesha Gamage was alive on 20 May 2012, her half-siblings take one-half of the collateral portion only and the ascendants take the other half per capita, which changes Kavindu's, Piyumi's and Lochana's fractions and adds a taker to the pedigree. The provision is marked partially_verified for that reason.

researcher_position: The general law applies because nothing in the facts brings the family within Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Thesawalamai.
verifier_position: Confirmed that 15-1876/s2 only carves those systems out and that the corpus holds no provision positively applying the general law to a given family. The Kandyan Succession Ordinance 23-1917 and the Muslim Intestate Succession Ordinance 10-1931 are both in the corpus and either would displace the map end to end. Stating the assumption in the gold answer is the right handling, but every share depends on it.

researcher_position: The 'tea estate' definition in s.25 of the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act applied in its 'not less than one hundred acres' form in October 2020, so the answer can state that threshold as the rule.
verifier_position: The corpus records that Act No. 20 of 2005 s.10(c) substitutes 'twenty hectares' for 'forty hectares' in that definition and that the substitution could not be applied because the as-enacted baseline reads 'one hundred acres'. The threshold in force at the matter date is therefore unknown from the corpus and is on the face of the 2005 Act twenty hectares, about forty-nine acres, not one hundred acres. The conclusion that a twenty acre property is not a tea estate survives either way, but the rule as stated in the gold answer is probably wrong.

researcher_position: No stamp duty authority for a conveyance is in the corpus, because Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.4 does not list a deed of transfer among the specified instruments and conveyance duty is a provincial levy; the step therefore rests only on Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6).
verifier_position: The rate is indeed outside the corpus, but the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 is in the corpus and s.13 of the 2006 Act expressly keeps it operative for instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property. Section 22(2) of the 1982 Act puts a duty on the attesting notary to take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which stamp duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed, and s.24(b) makes the duty payable by the grantee. Those are steps this notary must take and they were missed.

researcher_position: The consent required is that of the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Board.
verifier_position: Act No. 20 of 2005 s.3 renamed the Act and the Board to the Tea, Rubber and Coconut Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act and Board. The corpus edition keeps the 1958 names because the renaming is a body-wide substitution that was recorded as not applied, so the answer's naming is an artefact of the corpus edition rather than the law at the matter date.

researcher_position: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 (PROV-M065-008) is post-matter-date text throughout, so applicable_to_matter_date is false and the provision can only be supporting.
verifier_position: The words the map actually quotes are the opening scope words of section 2, including the carve-out for a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month. Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2 repealed only the words from "shall be of force" to the end, and No. 4 of 2024 s.2 renumbered the section and rewrote paragraphs (a) and (b). The quoted words therefore stood at October 2020 and applicable_to_matter_date should read true. Only the notarial-execution limb, which the map does not quote, is post-date. The subsection label "(1)" also comes from the 2024 renumbering. The provision can stay supporting, but the reason given for that role is wrong.

researcher_position: The pre-2022 wording of rule (9) survives verbatim inside 31-2022/s16 but was left as a note in the research notes rather than made a provision, and PROV-M065-022 quotes the post-2022 text with applicable_to_matter_date false.
verifier_position: Because that wording is quotable from the corpus, it should be a provision in its own right so that the identification point in question 1 rests on October 2020 text rather than on a post-date substitute. Added as PROV-M065-903. The lawyer should confirm that quoting an amending Act's recital of repealed words is an acceptable citation form for this benchmark.

researcher_position: Civil Procedure Code s.554X shows that a sealed duplicate or certified copy of the letters of administration issued in District Court Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T may be relied on in place of the original.
verifier_position: s.554X is in the FOREIGN PROBATES chapter (ss.554U-554BB); with the interpretation in s.554BB it governs only probate or letters of administration granted by a foreign court and resealed in Sri Lanka. It says nothing about a domestic District Court grant. Civil Procedure Code s.545 is the provision that makes the grant or certificates of heirship a document the purchaser must see.

researcher_position: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.16 is cited for the proposition that notarial deeds are executed in triplicate, flagged only as amended in 2022 and used as background.
verifier_position: The word triplicate was substituted by Act No. 30 of 2022 s.5; at 2020-04 the section read in duplicate. The Q03 rule paragraph states the post-matter-date rule as if it applied to this matter, which is a temporal error in the gold prose, not merely a background flag.

researcher_position: Section 27's one-side limb applies to the collateral half created by s.25, giving Kanthi 3/32, Manel 3/32, Upul 1/32 and Wimal 1/32.
verifier_position: The verifier accepts this reading, since s.25 admits only the paternal half-blood where the mother survives and s.27's final limb is expressly written for half-siblings of one side. But s.27 sits immediately after s.26 (both parents failing), and a reading that treats the s.25 collateral half as divided equally per capita among all four siblings (1/16 each) is arguable and would change every fraction. The point is flagged rather than resolved.

researcher_position: Rule 31(29) and section 4A carry no amendment events relevant to the matter, so both temporal notes say the provisions were untouched.
verifier_position: Rule 31(29) was amended by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3(9) (Form F to Form F 1), and section 4A was inserted by Notaries (Amendment) Law No. 20 of 1976 s.4. Neither changes the April 2020 position of the words actually relied on, but the notes as written overstate the position, and the first corpus_gaps entry repeats the rule (29) error.

researcher_position: Rule 31(22) bars Nimal Perera from attesting the father's execution in Kandy because Colombo and Kandy are different areas of authorised practice.
verifier_position: The corpus supports the rule but not the geography: nothing in the Notaries Ordinance as held here defines the judicial zones, so the step from 'practising in Colombo' to 'not authorised in Kandy' rests on facts outside the corpus. The conclusion is very likely right, but a lawyer should confirm the zone boundaries as at April 2020.

researcher_position: The corpus text of s.31 rule (30) incorporates the 2022 and 2024 amendments, and the April-2020 rule referred to the registered power of attorney.
verifier_position: The corpus consolidation of rule (30) is stale, not current: 31-2022 s.16(13) substituted the tail of the rule from the words 'he shall preserve a true copy of the registered power of attorney with his protocol' and 6-2024 s.3(10) substituted it again, and neither substitution appears in the corpus text, which still reads 'preserve a true copy of the power of attorney with his protocol, and shall forward a like copy with the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands'. The corpus text is therefore older even than the April-2020 rule, which per the words quoted in the 2022 Act required a copy of the registered power of attorney. The opening limb the answer relies on is unaffected either way.

researcher_position: The element relied on, that a deed may be signed by the executant or by a person duly authorised by him, is the long-standing content of s.2, so the post-2022 wording can be quoted safely for an April-2020 answer.
verifier_position: The corpus copy of Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Act No. 30 of 2022 s.2 sets out the paragraph (a) it inserted in full, and it contains no authorised-signatory limb; that limb entered the section only through Act No. 4 of 2024 s.2(2)(a). The proposition is probably right for April 2020, since 17-1852/s2 recites the pre-2022 Prevention of Frauds formula and expressly contemplates signature 'by some person lawfully authorized by him', but it cannot be established from the section text the map quotes.

researcher_position: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.12 is indispensable and the question is a three-hop question.
verifier_position: The charge-for-debt exception is expressed in s.11 itself, in the words other than and except charges and directions for the payment of any debt or debts, and s.11 already admits the attesting witness to prove execution and validity. Section 12 therefore confirms an attesting creditor's competence and adds nothing the conclusion depends on; it is supporting, and the hop count is 2.

researcher_position: The charged debt and the executor's commission are legitimate enrichment facts that make the scenario concrete.
verifier_position: They introduce two statutory issues, under ss.12 and 13, that the original three-mark question did not raise, so the enrichment widens the legal issue rather than supplying the missing party, relationship and document facts. Sections 10 and 11 alone answer what was asked.

researcher_position: Section 13 provides that attesting does not make an executor incompetent as a witness.
verifier_position: The first limb of s.13 makes a person competent notwithstanding that he is an executor; it does not make the competence turn on the act of attesting. Only the second limb, on the recompense or commission, is tied to attesting.

researcher_position: On the stated facts the brothers still hold undivided one third shares of the 45 perch portion, so the Schedule must describe the whole portion and the deed convey an undivided one third; the divided block description is the alternative.
verifier_position: Part (iii) as set describes the subject as "Anuk's divided block of land", so the description the question asks for is more likely the divided block defined by its own particular boundaries and extent under rule (16)(b) and s.13(2), with the undivided share as the alternative. The order of the two limbs in the gold answer may be inverted.

researcher_position: No amendment event touches paragraph (b) of rule (16), so the corpus text is the April 2020 text.
verifier_position: Act No. 31 of 2022, s.16(9)(b) substituted the words from "which it is a share: Provided, however" to the end of paragraph (b), so the April 2020 paragraph contained a proviso the corpus does not reproduce and whose effect on a post-partition description is unknown.

researcher_position: Section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance is marked applicable_to_matter_date=false and recorded as a corpus gap, because the corpus carries the text as amended by Act No. 30 of 2022 and Act No. 4 of 2024 and the April 2020 wording is said not to be in the corpus.
verifier_position: Both amending Acts are in the corpus and neither touches the words excerpted at PROV-M078-009. 30-2022 s.2 repealed only from the words shall be of force to the end of the section; 4-2024 s.2 renumbered the section, replaced paragraphs (a) and (b) of the renumbered subsection (1) and added subsection (2). The excerpted opening words stood in April 2020, so the provision is applicable and this is not a corpus gap. The boolean field was left untouched because it is outside what the verifier may edit; the correction is recorded in the verifier_note and corpus_gaps.

researcher_position: The Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 was set aside in full because section 13 of Act No. 12 of 2006 displaces it for instruments other than transfers of immovable property, motor vehicles and court documents.
verifier_position: Section 13 displaces the 1982 Act only in so far as it is inconsistent with the 2006 Act. Section 16 of the 1982 Act, on how a bond or mortgage for money to be lent is charged where the amount secured is limited or unlimited, has no counterpart in the 2006 Act and speaks directly to the mode of calculation that M078-Q03 asks for. Whether it survives is a legal judgement, not a corpus question. It does not unblock M078-Q03, because the 1982 Act also charges duty only at the prescribed rate and no rate table is in the corpus.

researcher_position: Sections 27 and 30 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance were inserted by section 4 of the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act, No. 22 of 1958.
verifier_position: 22-1958 s.4 substituted a heading in Chapter V of the principal enactment and inserted no section. The bracketed marker the corpus prints against sections 27 and 30 is that heading marker. Both sections are recorded as in force from 1927 with no amendment event, which is the sound basis for applying them at 2020-04, so the conclusion is unaffected but the stated reason is wrong.

researcher_position: Jaffna Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.6 required Mohan Nadaraja's written consent to Deed of Transfer No. 456 of 3 February 2015, and Lots 5A and 5B were Mala Nadaraja's thediatheddam under s.19(a).
verifier_position: These two characterisations are mutually exclusive on the corpus text. Section 6 governs property a wife held at marriage or acquired during marriage by gift, inheritance or conversion of such property, while s.19(a) defines thediatheddam as property acquired for valuable consideration that does not represent her separate estate. If the lots are thediatheddam, s.6 does not on its face require consent; if the purchase money came from her separate estate, they are separate estate and s.19 and s.20 do not apply. Nothing in the corpus resolves whether a wife's thediatheddam is subject to the same consent requirement.

researcher_position: Civil Procedure Code s.582, read with ss.585 and 502, means that a certificated curator and not the minor had to be joined as executant of Deed of Transfer No. 1234 of 1 August 2014.
verifier_position: Section 582 confers a right to apply for a certificate and bars an uncertificated person only from instituting or defending an action connected with the minor's estate. It says nothing about executing a deed. Section 502 is limited to its own chapter, which is not the chapter containing ss.582 and 585. The joinder requirement and the requirement of District Court sanction for a sale of a minor's land are Roman-Dutch common law and are not in this corpus.

researcher_position: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 supports the proposition that every dealing in the chain had to be notarially executed between 2008 and 2018.
verifier_position: The excerpt relied on is verbatim but stops before the operative words. The notarial-execution requirement in the corpus text sits in paragraph (a) as substituted by Act No. 30 of 2022 and read with Act No. 4 of 2024. The version in force for these deeds is not held, so s.2 can support the proposition only as background, and it does not list a gift among the dealings named.

researcher_position: Section 2 of Act No. 5 of 2017 is exhaustive both as to the ground (gross ingratitude) and as to the mode (an order of a competent court), so no other route to revocation survives.
verifier_position: The word only in s.2 attaches grammatically to the mode, only on an Order made by a competent court. The section states the ground for which the remedy is given but does not in terms say that no other ground exists. That gross ingratitude is the only statutory ground follows from the corpus sweep, not from the wording of s.2; whether the Act also ousts the Roman-Dutch grounds for revoking a donation is outside the corpus.

researcher_position: Section 6 defines Registrar of Lands and so fixes the officer to whom the s.4(1) lis pendens application is addressed.
verifier_position: Section 6 keys the Registrar of Lands to the district in which the land forming the subject matter of the deed is situated, while s.4(1)(a) directs the application to the Registrar of the district in which the deed is registered. The two tests diverge where a deed was registered in a district other than the one in which the land lies. On these enriched facts both are Gampaha, so the answer is unaffected, but the definition should not be cited as the source of the addressee rule.

researcher_position: The Western Province stamp duty rate is fixed by subsidiary instrument under ss.76 and 77 of Statute No. 6 of 1990.
verifier_position: s.76 empowers the Minister to specify the description of stamps to be used and to extend the s.39(4) exemption to other governments; the power to prescribe is s.77(1)(a). The conclusion that the rate lies outside the corpus is unaffected. Corrected in block_reason; the same wording remains in corpus_gaps, which is outside the verifier's edit scope.

researcher_position: Duty on the Deed of Gift is payable by the grantee under s.51(a) unless the deed provides otherwise.
verifier_position: Correct as to primary incidence but incomplete: under s.52(1) and (3) every person executing the instrument, including the donor, is liable to the Commissioner if it is not duly stamped, notwithstanding s.51, with recovery under s.52(2).

researcher_position: The Application paragraph advises that the caveat should describe the land, with its boundaries and the volume and folio, presented as the October 2019 position.
verifier_position: No corpus text in force at October 2019 imposes that content requirement. s.32(1) requires only a caveat in the prescribed form, and the Second Schedule that would fix the form's content is not in the corpus. The boundaries-and-volume-and-folio requirement is the language of Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act No. 32 of 2022 s.2(1)(b)(iv), which the map itself correctly excludes as post-dating the matter. The sentence should be struck or resourced by a lawyer; the verifier may not rewrite gold prose.

researcher_position: CL-M082-Q01-002 states as a direct rule that the prescribed caveat form is a form of the Second Schedule.
verifier_position: s.50 says only that the forms contained in the Second Schedule are to be used and may be altered by regulation, and s.49 makes prescribed mean prescribed by regulation. The Second Schedule is absent from the corpus, so that the caveat form sits in it rather than in a regulation made under s.49 is an inference. It is a plausible one, since 32-2022 s.2 places the caveat in Form VIII of that Schedule, but that is 2022 evidence for a 2019 proposition. Claim marked disputed.

researcher_position: Rule (24) of s.31 is a supporting provision that shows the Ordinance itself protects the confidentiality of a will.
verifier_position: Rule (24) prescribes what a notary enters in his own protocol register and says nothing about disclosure to third parties; it is background reinforcement at best, and rule (20)(h)(ii), inserted in 2022 and requiring the testator's name in the deed register, shows the Ordinance does not treat every will detail as secret in the notary's own records.

researcher_position: The children's status as prospective heirs gives them no entitlement to the information because while the testator lives they have no interest in his estate at all (CL-M083-Q01-006, and the same sentence in the gold answer).
verifier_position: The first half follows from rule (1), since the children are not the employer, but the proposition that a prospective heir has no interest in a living testator's estate is a rule of succession law and no provision in the corpus states it; it should not appear in a statute-only gold answer without a lawyer's authority.

researcher_position: Section 34 can be cited as supporting authority for the penal enforcement of rule (1), with a caveat that the fine figures come from a 2022 amendment.
verifier_position: The entire section in the corpus is the 2022 replacement, so the corpus supports no statement at all about the penalty in force in October 2019; a caveat inside the gold answer prose about which corpus text is being used is also out of place in a model answer.

researcher_position: The rule (9) text in force in October 2019 can be taken from the words recited as replaced in 31-2022/s16(6), so that amending subsection is recorded as an applicable provision.
verifier_position: The recital is reliable evidence of the replaced words and no intervening amendment held in the corpus touched rule (9), so the substance is right; but recording a 2022 amending subsection as applicable_to_matter_date true overstates the status of the instrument, and the map should be read as resting on the recited words alone until a lawyer checks a pre-2022 edition.

researcher_position: The answer is given for Lots 2 and 3 only, Lot 1 having been gifted away in 2005 and sold in 2013, with the alternative outcome for Lot 1 stated in the conclusion.
verifier_position: The corpus holds nothing on reserved life interests, so which of Kanthi Perera and Amali Perera could have sold Lot 1 in 2013, and what passed by that sale, cannot be settled from statute; the alternative should be treated as live rather than as a footnote to a single gold answer.

researcher_position: s.35 was considered and set aside because Lot 1 was gifted subject to a life interest and had left the estate, and the questions ask only for the pedigree and the present shares.
verifier_position: s.35 is in the corpus, was checked and is at least arguable: Amali Perera received Lot 1 from her mother in 2005 and became an heir to the same parent in 2014, which is the situation the section addresses, and if collation applied the children's shares would not be equal.

researcher_position: Section 9 of Act No. 12 of 2006 is indispensable to M088-Q02, and because the premises are at Nawala Road, Rajagiriya, the Provincial Council entitled to this lease duty under s.9 is the Western Provincial Council.
verifier_position: Section 9 is background only. It operates on duty 'payable to a Provincial Council in respect of documents and instruments referred to in List I of the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution'. Whether lease duty is such a duty cannot be established from the corpus, and the one provincial instrument in the corpus points the other way: 6-1990/s37 charges instruments of transfer of immovable property, documents filed in court and motor vehicle transfers in the Western Province, and does not charge leases. The verified answer to 'to whom do you pay' on these facts is the prescribed bank under s.8(2), with the Act administered by the Commissioner-General under s.2.

researcher_position: Claim CL-M088-Q02-006: because the lease concerns immovable property, the duty on it is paid to a prescribed bank and the bank's certificate is affixed to the lease agreement.
verifier_position: Section 8(2) says the duty 'may be paid' to a prescribed bank; it is an alternative to the general adhesive-stamp route in s.8(1), not the only lawful route. The claim as drafted states a permissive provision as mandatory and is marked disputed.

researcher_position: PROV-M088-009 records that the quoted words of 7-1840/s2 predate the 2022 and 2024 amendments and are unaffected by them.
verifier_position: Agreed as to the quoted words: 30-2022 s.2 repealed only from 'shall be of force' onwards, and the excerpt stops before that phrase. But the consequence the claims draw, that the deed must be in writing and notarially executed and attested, sits in the repealed-and-substituted part, so the April 2019 wording of that requirement is not in the corpus at all. The claims are left verified because 7-1840/s19 and 17-1852/s2 both recite the requirement and are unamended, but the primary text for the matter date is missing.

researcher_position: Municipal Councils Ordinance s.37(1)(b) read with the s.327 definition of "street" establishes that once Lot R1 is vested in the Council the public have a right of way over it, so M089-Q03 is answerable from statute alone and can be a proposed_gold item.
verifier_position: Section 327 makes a public right of way a criterion of being a "street", and the definition is inclusive ("includes"), so vesting does not itself confer the public right of way. Section 71(6) has to extend the word for its own section precisely because the general definition carries that requirement. The conclusion is probably correct as a matter of law, but it rests on an assumed premise that Lot R1 was vested as a street, which no corpus provision supplies.

researcher_position: The s.327 definition of "premises" is a supporting provision for M089-Q02, giving statutory recognition that a servitude is part of the property to which it appertains.
verifier_position: It is an interpretation clause opening with "In this Ordinance, unless the context otherwise requires", so it cannot support a general proposition of servitude law between private parties. Its role is background only.

researcher_position: The original is the instrument that goes forward for registration, and the notary must present the original at the land registry for the Nuwara Eliya division (gold_answer_draft rule and application; CL-M091-Q01-006 and CL-M091-Q01-013).
verifier_position: The registry is correctly identified by Registration of Documents Ordinance s.14(1), but s.26(2) of the same Ordinance provides that either the original or a duly attested or certified copy of the instrument may be presented for registration, so it is wrong to say the original is the instrument that must go forward. Both claims marked disputed and PROV-M091-901 added.

researcher_position: The 'Form F 1' wording of rules (26)(a)(i) and (29) is quoted as the excerpt with the anachronism flagged only in the temporal_note and in the research notes; the question is still offered as proposed_gold.
verifier_position: Two indispensable provisions carrying text that did not exist at the matter date is enough to keep the question out of gold until a lawyer either accepts the substitution as immaterial or supplies the April 2019 'Form F' wording. Marked partially_verified and the question downgraded.

researcher_position: Neglect of these duties exposes the notary to prosecution (CL-M091-Q01-015), citing s.37 and s.33, with s.34 carried as supporting context marked not applicable to the matter date.
verifier_position: Section 37 supports prosecution only for failure to register after instructions and funds. For breach of rules (24), (26) and (29) the penal provision in force in April 2019 is s.34 as it stood before the Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022, which the corpus does not hold. PROV-M091-011 marked unresolved and the claim marked disputed.

researcher_position: A warrant expressed as 'Colombo' does not reach Mount Lavinia, so s.31 rule (22) bars this notary from attesting at the bedside; the territorial point is supplied as a scenario fact because the corpus cannot settle it.
verifier_position: The corpus does address it. Sections 3(1) and 4(2) entitle a notary to a warrant for the judicial zone in which he resides, and s.4A deems a warrant expressed for a judicial division to authorise practice in that whole judicial zone. The notary resides at Battaramulla and holds a Colombo warrant, so the more natural reading is that his area is a judicial zone rather than the city, and Mount Lavinia may well fall inside it. If it does, rule (22) is not engaged and he may attend the bedside and attest himself, which is the opposite of the proposed conclusion.

researcher_position: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.4(2) is quoted in its current form but relied on only for the signature, notary and two-witness elements, which were in force in April 2019.
verifier_position: Act No. 30 of 2022 s.3 repealed all the words of s.4 from 'in the manner hereinafter mentioned' to the end and added subsection (2) in its place. Every word the answer relies on for the mode of execution is therefore 2022 text, and the April 2019 wording is nowhere in the corpus. The proposition may well be right as law, but it is not verifiable here.

researcher_position: FACT-M092-Q01-002 supplies the territorial premise and names an available notary for the client's area, so that the alternative route is determinate.
verifier_position: The examiner's facts (licensed for Colombo, resident at Battaramulla, client at Mount Lavinia) are the question. Stipulating that the warrant does not reach Mount Lavinia, and supplying a second notary who is warranted for it, answers the question in the background rather than in the analysis.

researcher_position: The notary should cause the search under s 31 rule (17)(a) and obtain a certified extract of the relevant folio, citing Registration of Documents Ordinance s 42.
verifier_position: In April 2019 s 42 conferred only a right, subject to prescribed regulations, for an interested person or his agent to search and to obtain certified copies or extracts. The obligation on a notary to obtain a certified extract of the folio containing the last entry was created by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s 16(10)(a), inserting rule (17)(b)(i). Presenting the extract as a required step states the post-2022 position.

researcher_position: Because the 2016 bond is registered and takes priority under Registration of Documents Ordinance s 7(1), the notary must require its discharge, or a release of the fifteen acres, before the deed is drawn.
verifier_position: Section 7(1) fixes priority between instruments; it imposes no duty on a notary, and no other cited provision requires him to insist on discharge or release before drafting. The step is sound conveyancing practice but it is not carried by the map's statutory citations.

researcher_position: The pre-drafting steps include having the fifteen-acre block surveyed and the blocking out plan approved.
verifier_position: Section 23A(1) only forbids an officer of a local authority to approve a blocking out plan of such an estate without the Board's certificate under s 14. It does not require approval of the plan before the deed is drafted, and the local-authority approval machinery is outside the corpus. The survey is required in substance by rule (16)(b), not by Survey Act s 13, which is an admissibility rule.

researcher_position: Section 39 (District Court power to cancel or rectify a registration) was considered and rejected in the research notes as confined to forgery and registration without authority, and it was left out of the legal map altogether.
