verifier_position: Section 39 also reaches an instrument registered in contravention of any provision of the Ordinance, and by section 14(2) a mis-folioed registration is not duly registered under Chapter III. The court route is therefore at least arguable and should appear as a background provision so that the gold answer's statement that no court order is required is a reasoned choice rather than a silent one.

researcher_position: CL-M098-Q02-009 states that the applicant must produce Deed No. 351, Plan No. 251, Plan No. 255 and an extract of Vol/Folio A 350/25.
verifier_position: Section 35(1) requires only that the error be shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar-General. The particular list of documents is Land Registry practice and is supported by no provision in the corpus; the claim is marked disputed rather than deleted.

researcher_position: CL-M098-Q03-003 renders the section 106 definition of value as the price in the opinion of the revenue officer.
verifier_position: Section 106 says in the opinion of the Assessor, and defines Assessor as a Provincial Assessor of Revenue, a different office from the Commissioner. A gold claim should say Assessor and reach the Commissioner through section 104(4).

researcher_position: The nurse should be refused as a witness because she cannot make the declaration of acquaintance contemplated by rule (9) and cannot supply from her own knowledge the particulars of the testator that rule (20)(c) requires the attestation to carry, even though the Notary's own knowledge of the testator meets the identification limb of rule (9).
verifier_position: On the October 2018 wording the vetting and declaration duty in rule (9) was introduced by the words 'and in the latter case', so it applied where the notary relied on the attesting witnesses' knowledge of the executant. This Notary knows the testator, so the corpus does not show that duty to be owed on these facts, and rule (20)(c) supplies no independent ground because it calls for the full names and residences of the attesting witnesses themselves. Refusing the nurse is sound practice and may well be what the pre-2022 rule (20)(b) required, but the corpus as it stands does not carry it as a duty.

researcher_position: Rule (10) is recorded as a corpus gap, but the answer is still put forward as proposed gold.
verifier_position: Rule (10) sat between the identification rule (9) and the reading-over rule (11) and was repealed only in 2024 without being reproduced; the pre-2022 wording of rule (20)(b), the witness-facing attestation paragraph, is lost in the same way. A gold answer to a question that asks for the precautions relating to witnesses should not be fixed until a 2018 print of the Ordinance is consulted.

researcher_position: Rule (14) of s.31 is carried as supporting only, on the footing that a duty in similar terms to ascertain full names before signing existed before 2022, and the gold answer's rule paragraph states s.31(14) as part of the law the notary must follow.
verifier_position: The corpus holds only the 31-2022 s.16(7) text of rule (14). The map cannot both disclaim its temporal applicability and state it in the gold answer's rule paragraph as applicable law. Either the pre-2022 wording is obtained from outside the corpus, or the rule (14) sentence comes out of the answer and CL-M101-Q01-008 is reduced to rule (18).

researcher_position: FACT-M101-Q01-008 ('Ranjith's left thumb is intact and an impression of it can be taken') is a synthetic_decisive fact needed because rule (15) specifies the left thumb.
verifier_position: Naming the left thumb in the scenario hands the candidate the distinctive step of rule (15). A neutral formulation ('both his hands are uninjured') would supply the same fact without leaking the answer. The same objection applies more weakly to FACT-M101-Q01-007's 'can write their names', which telegraphs rule (8).

researcher_position: s.34 may be cited as supporting authority, marked applicable_to_matter_date false, because the answer does not turn on the size of the fine; the gold prose accordingly says that breach of rule (1) is an offence punishable on summary trial under s.34(1)(a).
verifier_position: A provision marked inapplicable at the matter date should not appear in the rule statement of the gold answer as though it were the law in October 2018. 31-2022 s.17 repealed the whole of the old s.34, so neither the framing of the offence nor the paragraph lettering used in the prose can be sourced to the corpus for 2018. Either the pre-2022 s.34 is added to the corpus or the two sentences resting on it come out of the prose.

researcher_position: The testator is the notary's employer for the permission exception, on the ordinary meaning of the word plus the added facts.
verifier_position: Probably right in practice, but employer is undefined in the Ordinance (defs 1-1907 returns only Council of Legal Education, High Court Judge and Registrar-General), so the identification cannot be verified from the corpus. The conclusion does not depend on it: the children plainly are not the notary's employer and nobody has given permission, so the exception fails on any reading. The claim should not be presented as a verified statutory application.

researcher_position: 15-1876 s.33 (illegitimate children) was rejected in the research notes and left out of the map, on the ground that Achini is described as a daughter by a first wife and is therefore a lawful child of Nimal.
verifier_position: The conclusion is probably right, but s.33 is the operative exception to the children's preferent right in s.24 and belongs in the map as background, so a lawyer can see that Achini's whole 86/1152 depends on s.33 not biting. Added as PROV-M106-902.

researcher_position: 15-1876 s.30 is cited for per capita division at every step, including the division of the second half of Bimal's sibling portion among Amal, Krishni and Achini.
verifier_position: The excerpt omits s.30's opening words "Except when otherwise expressly provided,". Section 27 does expressly provide otherwise for the first half of the sibling portion, so s.30 can carry only the divisions s.27 leaves open. The figures are unchanged but the reasoning as written overstates s.30.

researcher_position: Under the final limb of s.27 the second half of Bimal's sibling portion is divided per capita among Amal, Krishni and Achini, giving 7/576 each.
verifier_position: Section 27 says only that the full siblings "divide the other half with the half-brothers and sisters" and does not state the proportion. The per capita reading is the natural one on s.30 and is what the corpus supports, but a split between the full-blood group and the half-blood group would give different figures and nothing in the corpus forecloses it. This is the single point on which the 203/203/86/84 answer could move.

researcher_position: Section 13 was last amended in 1982, so the consolidated corpus text of section 13(1) is the text in force at the April 2018 reference date, and the schedule requirements are the district, the village/pattu/korale or other division, and, for land in a town, the street name.
verifier_position: Section 13(1) was repealed and substituted by Act No. 48 of 2011, s.2, in force at the reference date. The list is wider: District, Pattu, Korale, Divisional Secretary's Division, local authority division, Grama Niladari Division and village, and for land in a municipality, town or developed area the number as well as the street name. The corpus edition of the principal Ordinance is a 1990 consolidation, which is why the 2011 substitution is not reflected in it; the amending Act is in the corpus and section 13 shows latest_change_year 1982, which is what led the researcher astray.

researcher_position: The corpus does not expose the wording of Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16) as it stood in April 2018, so the rule is supporting only and not applicable to the matter date.
verifier_position: The corpus does expose it. Act No. 47 of 2011, s.2 substituted paragraph (a) of rule (16) and its as-enacted text is in the corpus; the next changes to section 31 are 2022 and 2024. Paragraph (a) as at April 2018 is therefore available. Only paragraph (b), which the 2011 Act did not touch, remains unconfirmable for the reference date.

researcher_position: Section 13(7) requires a reference to the volume and folio of an earlier instrument relating to the same land to be written at the head of the deed presented for registration.
verifier_position: The duty is conditional. The corpus body continues 'if such reference is known to the notary who prepared the instrument, or, if the instrument was not prepared by a notary, if such reference is known to the person presenting the instrument for registration'. The excerpt was cut before the condition, and claims CL-M107-Q04-006 and CL-M107-Q04-013 state the duty unconditionally.

researcher_position: The answer is in two parts: Gihan may have the deed drawn and attested and it may well be accepted for registration, but he takes nothing by it.
verifier_position: The first half is a prediction about registry practice rather than a statutory consequence. Nothing in the Ordinance obliges a Registrar to accept the deed either; s.36(1) is permissive ('may, if he thinks fit') and s.36(1)(b) lets him refuse an instrument that does not comply with any written law affecting its form or mode of execution. For a 2-mark question the safer gold is a flat 'no, he cannot lawfully acquire or register such an interest', with the registrability point kept as supporting nuance. The prose was left unchanged and the two claims that carry the prediction were marked disputed.

researcher_position: Apartment Ownership Law s.25 is indispensable because it resolves the conflict between that Law and the Registration of Documents Ordinance.
verifier_position: There is no conflict to resolve. The Ordinance does not purport to confer title, and s.7(4) denies the registration any effect on its own terms, so s.25 is a fallback rather than a step in the reasoning. Moved to supporting; hop count unchanged at 4.

researcher_position: Apartment Ownership Law s.11 is the central prohibition that defeats the Deed of Declaration.
verifier_position: s.11 restricts dealings with an existing share in the common elements. Gihan has no share, so the deed fails first under s.9(1) and s.9(5), which vest the common elements in the parcel owners and deem the person named in the registered plan the absolute owner. s.11 answers the further point that a half share of the land could never be held severed from a parcel. Kept as indispensable but the role is qualified.

researcher_position: The enriched scenario, in which the notary identifies a Japanese national by his passport and notes his full name from it, is a neutral concretisation of the facts, and the notary may attest the deed.
verifier_position: In April 2018 rule (9) of section 31 read "He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same be known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses thereto" - the words the 2022 Act replaced. Identification by the bio-page of a passport entered rule (9) only through Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6). The enriched facts do not say the executant was known to the notary or to the two witnesses, so on the April 2018 law the premise that he could attest at all is doubtful, and the fact is anachronistic.

researcher_position: FACT-M110-Q01-005 (the executant cannot read English) is a decisive fact that properly brings rule (11) into the answer.
verifier_position: The examined question is worth one mark and asks only about a signature in Japanese. Adding inability to read English creates a second, separate duty and enlarges the legal issue, which enrichment is not supposed to do. Rule (15) is the answer; rule (11) belongs to a different question.

researcher_position: Q04 cannot be answered because s.9 of the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act leaves the choice between the place of execution and the place where the property is situated to List I of the Ninth Schedule, which is not in the corpus.
verifier_position: The block is right on corpus text alone, but the choice may be settled outside the corpus: stamp duty on a transfer of immovable property is a devolved provincial levy tied to the situation of the land, which would select the Southern Provincial Council for a Matara land executed in Colombo. The corpus cannot decide this; a lawyer can.

researcher_position: Rule (6) of section 31 was not among the rules substituted by Act No. 47 of 2011, Act No. 31 of 2022 or Act No. 6 of 2024, so the quoted text stood in April 2018.
verifier_position: Rule (6) was substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(4). The substituted text is word for word what is quoted, so the quotation is almost certainly also the pre-2022 wording, but the corpus does not hold the pre-2022 text and cannot confirm it. The provision is supporting only, so this does not block any question.
